opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think memory is one of those things that's easy to underestimate until you've actually tried to build these systems. If you go back even a couple of years, the world models people were training, including our own earlier work, would hold things together for a few seconds. If you turned away from something and turned back, there was a good chance it would have changed or vanished. The model had no persistent notion that a world exists independently of where you're currently looking.

So getting to roughly a minute of visual memory with Genie 3 was a big step for us. Concretely, you can paint something on a wall, walk off, explore somewhere else, come back, and it's still there and still consistent. What I find most exciting is that we didn't hard-code that with an explicit 3D representation. It emerged from training at scale with the right architecture. That suggests consistency is something these models can learn, not something we have to bolt on.

I'd be careful not to overstate it, though. A minute is great for interactive exploration and for a lot of agent training scenarios, but it's nowhere near what you'd want long term. If you want an agent to learn a complex task that takes hours, or to live in a persistent world, you need much longer horizons, and you need memory that isn't only visual: things like game state, the consequences of actions, other agents' behavior.

So I see it as crossing a threshold where these models become genuinely useful as environments, both for people exploring them and for training embodied agents, rather than as an end point. The next frontier is pushing that horizon further while keeping things real-time and controllable, and those goals pull against each other. That trade-off is where a lot of the interesting research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response calls one minute a big step, but does not say it would have been considered an incredible achievement for Genie 1 or Genie 2.

r002.rationale: The response says one minute is too short for long-term goals, but does not predict that it will seem embarrassingly short in the future.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the memory piece is actually one of the things I'm most excited about, and it's worth stepping back to see why. When we did Genie 1, we were generating a couple of seconds of video at pretty low resolution, and the model had essentially no notion of persistence. If you turned the camera away and came back, the world had changed. Genie 2 pushed that out to maybe ten or twenty seconds, and you started to see some object permanence emerge, but it was fragile.

With Genie 3, you can now walk around a generated environment in real time, look away from something, and come back a minute or so later and it's still there, roughly where you left it. And the key thing for me is that we didn't build that in explicitly. There's no scene graph, no 3D representation we're maintaining under the hood. It's emergent from training the model to be a consistent world model at scale. So in that sense it feels a lot like what we saw with language models, where capabilities like in-context reasoning just showed up as you scaled things up properly.

Now, a minute is clearly not the end of the story. If you want these worlds to be useful for training agents, or for people to actually spend time in, you need consistency over hours, not minutes. And there's a real tension there, because a lot of what makes Genie 3 work is the autoregressive generation, which is inherently costly to extend. So I see the one-minute memory as a kind of existence proof. It shows that long-horizon consistency can come from the same recipe, and now the question becomes how far that recipe can be pushed versus whether you need new ideas.

The other thing I'd say is that memory is really the bottleneck for the thing I care most about, which is open-ended learning. If you want agents to learn in these worlds, the world has to remember what the agent did. Otherwise it's just a very impressive hallucination. So for me, this is less a video generation milestone and more a step toward environments that can actually support learning.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Genie 1’s few seconds and Genie 2’s fragile 10–20 seconds with Genie 3’s minute, but does not say that a minute would have been considered an incredible achievement for either earlier model.

r002.rationale: The response says a minute is not enough for some future uses and that consistency over hours is needed, but it does not predict that a minute will seem embarrassingly short in the future.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a meaningful step forward. With an interactive world model, you want more than a sequence of plausible images—you want the sense that there’s a world persisting as you move through it. If you look away from something and then come back, you expect it to still be there.

A minute of visual memory starts to let you explore that kind of consistency over longer interactions. But I wouldn’t interpret it as having solved persistent memory or world understanding. The interesting question is what the model retains, and how reliably it retains it as you change the scene. For me, that’s an important direction for progress: extending the time over which a generated world remains coherent while you interact with it.

r001.rationale: The response calls one minute a meaningful step forward, but does not say it would have been an incredible achievement for Genie 1 or Genie 2.

r002.rationale: The response discusses extending coherence over time, but does not predict that one minute will seem embarrassingly short in the future.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an exciting step, because the challenge isn’t just generating a convincing frame—it’s maintaining a coherent world as you interact with it. If you turn away from something and then come back, you want it to still be there, in the same place. That continuity is really important if these models are going to become useful environments for agents.

A minute is still a limited horizon, and visual memory isn’t the same as having a complete understanding of the world. But it gives us a meaningful window in which to study longer interactions: can an agent explore, take actions, and return to something it encountered earlier? For me, the exciting part is moving toward worlds that remain consistent enough for an agent to learn from experience.

r001.rationale: The response calls one minute a meaningful window, but does not say it would have been an incredible achievement for Genie 1 or Genie 2.

r002.rationale: It describes one minute as limited, but does not predict that it will seem embarrassingly short in the future.
